title: IB Predicted Grades vs Final Grades: What Changes?
summary: IB predicted grades vs final grades explained for students and parents: understand grade boundaries, university offers, and how to plan your next steps.
body_markdown:
IB predicted grades vs final grades compares two different measures: teachers’ evidence-based estimates and official assessed results. Predictions can inform university applications, but they do not guarantee or set the final result. Final grades follow marking, relevant moderation, and the application of grade boundaries.


Imagine Maya, a hypothetical DP student, seeing a predicted Biology grade of 6 beside a mock result of 5. Her parent asks which number is “right”. Both can be reasonable: one describes performance on a particular assessment; the other expresses a teacher’s judgement about the eventual outcome.


The useful question is what evidence supports each number and what to do next.


**A quick checklist:**


- Identify whether the number is a test grade, mock grade, prediction, or final result.
- Check the subject, Higher or Standard Level, and assessment coverage.
- Ask what evidence supports the prediction.
- Separate raw marks, weighted totals, and grades from 1-7.
- Read university offer conditions, including subject requirements.


### What IB predicted grades tell you


The IB defines a predicted grade as a teacher’s prediction of achievement, based on evidence of a candidate’s work and knowledge of IB standards. It is a professional judgement, rather than a universal calculation.


Evidence may include assessments, mock examinations, coursework progress, and sustained performance. Schools differ in how they combine evidence and when they issue predictions. A university application prediction may also be produced at a different point from the prediction submitted to the IB.


Ask when your school finalises predictions and whether later evidence can be considered. Knowing the timeline helps you plan assessments and teacher conversations. It also prevents confusion when two documents show predictions made at different stages.


Maya’s teacher might explain that her understanding supports a 6, while the mock exposed weak data analysis. That explanation identifies both the evidence and the remaining risk.


Read about[how IB predicted grades are calculated](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-are-ib-predicted-grades-calculated) , then check your school’s policy.


A student asks a fortune teller about the future while the fortune teller reads a stack of homework.


### How final IB grades are determined


Final subject grades reflect assessed achievement under the subject’s rules. The Diploma Programme uses external and internal assessment, with combinations and weightings depending on the subject. Internally assessed work is subject to external moderation.


Component marks contribute to a weighted subject total. Grade boundaries translate that total into a grade from 1-7. Across six subjects, students can earn 42 points, with up to three additional points from Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay. Receiving the diploma also requires meeting its other requirements.


When reviewing a practice result, check whether it includes every component and uses the correct weighting. A strong result on one paper gives useful evidence, but it cannot represent the whole subject by itself.


A predicted 6 adds no marks to an examination response. A predicted 5 does not prevent a final 6 or 7. The assessed work determines the outcome.


### Why predictions and final results differ


A prediction is made before all the evidence exists. Students can subsequently improve, lose consistency, or perform differently under examination conditions.


Someone may understand the content but leave questions unfinished. Another student may progress substantially after a disappointing mock. Coursework marks can be affected by moderation, while classroom assessments may sample only part of the syllabus.


Final results can be higher, lower, or unchanged. A discrepancy alone does not prove teacher carelessness or insufficient student effort.


Maya can ask: “Which parts of my work support a 6, and which still look like a 5?” This guide to[discussing a higher predicted grade with teachers](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/can-i-ask-my-teachers-to-give-me-a-higher-predicted-grade-in-ib-understanding-the-ethics-and-strategies) can help structure that conversation.


### How IB grade boundaries affect comparisons


A percentage becomes meaningful when you know what was assessed and which boundaries apply. No single percentage always earns a 7 across every subject, level, and examination session.


Boundaries can change between sessions as the IB maintains standards across assessments of differing difficulty. Check the subject, level, session, and assessment route or timezone where applicable.


Consider invented figures: Maya earns a weighted practice total of 68 out of 100. With an illustrative grade 6 boundary of 65, she reaches that grade. With a boundary of 70, she falls below it. Neither threshold is an official boundary or forecast.


A calculation can be exact for a selected boundary set without reliably predicting future results. RevisionDojo’s guide to[IB grade boundaries and result trends](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/insights-on-ib-grade-boundaries-and-result-trends) explains the context.


### What this means for university offers


Predicted grades help universities assess applications before final results arrive. Conditional offers specify what applicants must achieve. Requirements vary by institution, course, and country.


An illustrative offer might require 36 points overall and a 6 in Higher Level Biology. Meeting the total would not automatically satisfy the separate Biology condition.


If results miss an offer, check your application status and contact the university and school coordinator. Acceptance is not guaranteed, but families should not infer the decision from the shortfall alone.


### Turning a prediction into a revision plan


Maya’s task is now specific: improve data analysis, finish timed responses, and demonstrate progress consistently.


For the next week, she could complete one timed data question, review where marks were lost, and practise the same skill in a different context. Keeping a brief error log would help her distinguish missing knowledge from misread instructions or weak explanations. That record also gives her teacher concrete evidence to discuss at their next meeting.


RevisionDojo brings that process together as a comprehensive IB resource. Study Notes and Flashcards support knowledge review; the Questionbank targets particular skills. AI Chat can unpack explanations, while Grading tools provide feedback to consider alongside mark schemes and teacher guidance.


[RevisionDojo Mock Exams](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/revisiondojo-mock-exams) and Predicted Papers support timed practice without guaranteeing future examination content. The Coursework Library and Tutors offer support with assessed writing or persistent misunderstandings.


Try a task, inspect errors, revise the relevant material, and attempt a fresh question. This guide to[improving IB predicted grades](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-improve-your-predicted-grades-in-ib-or-practical-strategies-and-revisiondojo-support) develops that routine.


Maya’s prediction has not changed yet, but she understands her next step. Her parent can ask a more useful question: “What has your latest work shown you?”
